BIBLIOGRAPHIC RECORD

 Epictetus. (c.A.D. 50–c.A.D. 138).  The Golden Sayings of Epictetus.
The Harvard Classics.  1909–14.

CLXXVII

When a man prides himself on being able to understand and interpret the writings of Chrysippus,
 say to yourself:—
If Chrysippus had not written obscurely, this fellow would have had nothing to be proud of. But what is it that 
I
 desire? To understand Nature, and to follow her! Accordingly I ask who is the Interpreter. On hearing that it is Chrysippus, I go to him. But it seems I do not understand what he wrote. So I seek one to interpret that. So far there 
is nothing to pride myself upon. But when I have found my interpreter, what remains is to put in practice his instructions. This itself is the only thing to be proud of. But if I admire the interpretation and that alone, what else have I turned out but a mere commentator instead of a lover of wisdom?—except indeed that I happen to be interpreting Chrysippus instead of Homer. So when any one says to me, 
Prithee, read me Chrysippus,
 I am more inclined to blush, when I cannot show my deeds to be in harmony and accordance with his sayings.
